clinicalPearls: An X-linked proximal tubulopathy affecting mainly males, caused by variants in CLCN5 (Dent disease 1) or OCRL (Dent disease 2)
The defining feature is low-molecular-weight proteinuria, which is often the earliest and most consistent abnormality
Hypercalciuria is characteristic and drives nephrocalcinosis and recurrent nephrolithiasis
Additional proximal tubular dysfunction may include phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, glycosuria and impaired urinary acidification, at times amounting to a partial Fanconi syndrome
Progressive chronic kidney disease develops in many affected males, sometimes reaching kidney failure in adulthood
Dent disease 2 (OCRL) can show mild extrarenal features overlapping with Lowe syndrome, such as subclinical cataract or mild cognitive involvement
Female carriers may have milder manifestations such as low-molecular-weight proteinuria or hypercalciuria
reference.pathophysiology: Dent disease is an inherited disorder of the renal proximal tubule caused by loss of function of the endosomal chloride/proton exchanger encoded by CLCN5, or of the phosphatase encoded by OCRL. Both proteins are required for normal acidification and trafficking within the endocytic machinery that reabsorbs filtered low-molecular-weight proteins via the megalin-cubilin receptor system. Defective endosomal function impairs receptor-mediated endocytosis, so filtered proteins escape into the urine, producing the hallmark low-molecular-weight proteinuria. Associated disturbances of calcium and phosphate handling generate hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis and stones, and cumulative tubular and interstitial damage leads to progressive decline in kidney function.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome (e.g. cystinosis)
Distal renal tubular acidosis with nephrocalcinosis
additionalInvestigations: Quantification of low-molecular-weight proteinuria (e.g. urinary retinol-binding protein or beta-2-microglobulin relative to creatinine)
Urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio to document hypercalciuria
Renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and stones
Assessment of proximal tubular function including phosphate, glucose, amino acids and acid-base status
Genetic testing of CLCN5 and OCRL
Serial measurement of kidney function to monitor progression
redFlags: Recurrent obstructing renal stones or symptomatic nephrocalcinosis
Growth failure in a child suggesting significant tubular or renal impairment
Features suggesting evolving extrarenal disease in OCRL-related cases
reference.prognosis: Dent disease is slowly progressive; many affected males develop chronic kidney disease and a proportion reach kidney failure between the third and fifth decades, while proteinuria and hypercalciuria are usually present from childhood. Progression rate varies and extrarenal disease is generally mild.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because dipstick testing detects albumin poorly and misses low-molecular-weight proteinuria
Attributing recurrent stones to idiopathic hypercalciuria without checking for tubular proteinuria
Failing to distinguish Dent disease 2 from Lowe syndrome when OCRL is involved
Assuming female relatives are entirely unaffected
management: No disease-specific cure; management centres on reducing hypercalciuria with thiazide diuretics, with attention to avoiding volume depletion and hypokalaemia
Ensure generous fluid intake and consider citrate supplementation and dietary measures to limit stone formation and nephrocalcinosis
Replace proximal tubular losses and treat metabolic bone disease with phosphate and vitamin D supplementation where phosphaturia or rickets develops
Slow chronic kidney disease progression through blood-pressure control, cautious renin-angiotensin blockade and avoidance of nephrotoxic agents
Surveillance with serial kidney function, low-molecular-weight proteinuria, urinary calcium and renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and stones
Manage acute stone episodes and refer to urology for recurrent nephrolithiasis
Institute renal replacement therapy and transplantation for kidney failure, noting the tubulopathy does not recur in the allograft
Offer genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance and screen at-risk male relatives and carrier females
